en: One Fascicle of the Ritual Manual for the Practice of the Vajra One Vehicle of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Homage to the Tathāgata Vairocana, Ocean of Great Wisdom, and to the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi.
O Bodhisattva,
having received the holy decree of the Buddha,
I have ventured to consult the Sanskrit manuscripts and have thus briefly composed these secret ritual procedures for the three mysteries.
Therefore, it is now said that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni practiced the yoga of cultivation.
Those who wish to cultivate this Dharma should first give rise to the unsurpassed, right, and true mind,
and don the noble robe of patience.
Constantly reciting and chanting these three secret syllables— *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*— in accordance with them without contradiction,
one should then proceed to the presence of a yoga-ācārya. There,
by receiving the secret ritual manual and practicing the recitation, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
Vairocana said: "That ācārya,

if he sees a sentient being who is a fit vessel for the Dharma, free from all defilements, possessing great faith and understanding, diligent and courageous, with deep conviction, and constantly mindful of benefiting others— "
If a disciple possesses such characteristics as these,
the ācārya should go in person to exhort and inspire them.
Furthermore, there are two other kinds of disciples.
First, one who has already resolved upon bodhicitta;
the teacher goes to that disciple's place and exhorts them to advance.
Second, one who has not yet resolved upon bodhicitta.
The disciple goes to the teacher's presence to offer encouragement;
among them, one who is wise and most preeminent—
having recognized such a person, one may then transmit and bestow [the teachings].
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Buddha Vairocana, saying:
"I see that the Buddha’s form-body wears a great jewel crown;
within the crown appear the emblems of the five Buddhas, which are neither cause nor fruit."
Abiding in the great lunar disc within the space of the eternally quiescent light,
he constantly proclaims the secret teachings of the Vajra,
which cannot be known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Or, dwelling upon a lotus pedestal, he manifests the body of a Reward Buddha and further expounds the supreme secret Dharma of the Vajra One Vehicle: that the Dharma-realm is Mind-Only.
We, relying on the virtue of internal realization, constantly see and constantly hear it.
Only those who have newly set out on the path are deluded and do not understand.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will act for their benefit in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
"If the Buddha grants his permission,
I wish to proclaim the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, Śākyamuni,
so that all foolish people may attain the wisdom of a Buddha."
I only pray that the Tathāgata will preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, so that they may hear the wisdom of skillful means;
may he reveal the true mark to all sentient beings, causing them to awaken to the Vajrayāna and enter the gateway of the letter A.
Having spoken these words, Vairocana said:
"Excellent, Samantabhadra! You are able to know my mind."
May this cause me joy.
In the past, having practiced the three secret gates and realized the state of Vajradhara,
I sat upon the sublime seat of Vajra-Bodhi.
Having subdued all Māras and attained equal and perfect enlightenment,
many eons have passed since then; yet,
due to the merit of their past lives, sentient beings [have encountered this].
Although you have met me and seen me according to your capacity,
and heard me according to your faculties, as you see me now,
I attained perfect enlightenment at the summit of the form realm, in the fourth dhyāna.
He immediately descended from the summit of Mount Sumeru;
at the Great Vajra-Indra Mandala,
all the Tathāgatas requested me to turn the four wheels of the Dharma.
Within each wheel there are thirty-seven noble ones who,
abiding in the samādhi of non-compassion, subdue the various celestial Māras and cause them to enter right view.
Now is precisely the time.
Furthermore, desiring to expound the unsurpassed secret Dharma of the Mahāyāna,
the Tathāgata will subsequently enter the path of parinirvāṇa through the power of his secret supernatural faculties.
Do not recklessly proclaim this among those lacking wisdom; I now grant you permission.
You should quickly explain the method of manifesting my forms in accordance with the various classes of beings.
You must rely upon the ritual procedures of the true Dharma.
"What should be spoken and what should be kept secret.
Having said these words, he sat in silence.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi...
With a heart full of exultation,
he appeared before the assembly and spoke this Dharma:
"If one wishes to repay the benevolence of the Unsurpassed World-Honored One..."
First, construct a maṇḍala.
In its center, paint an image of Śākyamuni,
with a golden body endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Clad in the robes of a *kāṣāya*, he manifests the form of preaching the Dharma;
his hand of wisdom (*jñāna-hasta*) forms the *śrīvatsa* mudrā,
with the hand of principle (*tattva-hasta*) placed upward in front of the hand of wisdom.
He sits in the full lotus posture upon a white lotus pedestal;
Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Maitreya reside at the four corners,
as described in the *Tāizang* (Womb Realm).
Each sat upon a lotus flower in the half-lotus posture.
Before the Buddha was the Tathāgata’s almsbowl;
to the Buddha’s right was the auspicious vase (bhadraghaṭa) containing flowers.
Behind the Buddha is a mendicant’s staff (khakkhara),
and to the Buddha’s left is a precious conch shell;
each rests upon a lotus petal and is encircled by radiant flames.
Having completed the drawing of the maṇḍala,
one should practice in a secluded and silent place where sages attained the Way,
or in a pure chamber, or before a śarīra stūpa, or on a mountain peak, or beneath a tree.
Establish a maṇḍala in one location.
Next, prepare the altar site and arrange the ritual implements for adornment and offering;
these consist of six types: unguents, seasonal flowers, incense, food and drink, lamps, and arghya perfumed water.
There may be those with wisdom who offer the Dharma as their service;
they bathe their bodies three times each day and night,
or they take the light of reality (*tattva*) as water to sprinkle upon their crowns while contemplating the principle.
Whenever one arrives at a place of practice (doctrinal field), one performs prostrations.
There are three kinds of prostration:
the first is vocal prostration.
The second is mental worship;
the third is physical worship.
These constitute the prostrations of the three karmas.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
to utter the word "Namo" constitutes vocal salutation;
furthermore, even at all times when no sound is uttered, [the salutation is maintained].
To take refuge solely by contemplating the virtues of the World-Honored One within the mind, and to rejoice and take refuge—this is the mental prostration.

Furthermore, placing the five wheels upon the ground—the forehead, the two hands, and the two knees—and turning the divine mind is called a "wheel" (*cakra*); alternatively, joining the palms and bowing the head constitutes the physical prostration.
As for ritual propriety (*li*), it does not necessarily require one to cast the body to the ground;
rather, reverent devotion constitutes ritual propriety.
This is why one bows one's head to the ground.
Because one touches the feet of the World-Honored One, it is called "prostration.
Next is the repentance for karmic obstacles, consisting of both ritual and principle-based repentance.
Following that is the rejoicing in the virtues of the noble and the ordinary.
Next, request the Buddha to remain in the world;
then, perform the dedication of merit and make vows, followed by extensive offerings.
Thereafter, engage in recitation and the turning of Mahāyāna sūtras as you see fit.
If one abides in this Dharma, all necessities will be fulfilled;
without changing this very body, one shall behold the form-body of the Buddha,
and in birth after birth, one shall remain free from all evil realms.
One will constantly attain the virtue of promoting the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings,
swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and achieve success according to one's faculties.
If they seek the fruit of immortality,
the Buddha manifests as the seer Gautama and preaches the Dharma for them.
If one seeks the Mahāyāna,
Samantabhadra manifests his body and preaches the Dharma for them.
Gradually entice them and lead them into the Buddha-way.
Next, explain the mudrā: the Tathāgata’s Alms-bowl Mudrā.
First, place the right hand at the heart with the palm facing upward.
Next, place the palm of the left hand over the palm of the right hand.
Let the tip of the left little finger touch the tip of the right thumb, and let the tip of the left thumb touch the tip of the right little finger. The mudrā and mantra are as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ lokapālādhiṣṭhitadhara dhara mahānābhabuddhapātra svāhā.* This dharma-seal mantra possesses great vigor.
One shall always be protected by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas.
One should form this mudrā and recite this mantra once;
finally, one should call to mind sentient beings in the hells and the hungry ghost realm, reciting [the name] one hundred and eight times.
Then one will obtain all manner of food, such that all hungry ghosts in the hells are fully satiated.
If one travels through wildernesses, by likewise binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra,
one will ensure that no spirits or demons in the wilderness cause any disturbance.
If one wishes to cause the bowl to fly, one should likewise employ this mudrā and mantra.
Next is the Tathāgata Amṛta Mudrā:
with the right hand, [place] the thumb...
Cross the thumbs, index fingers, middle fingers, ring fingers, and little fingers over the top.
The mantra is as before:
*Oṃ jñānini buddhadhāni svāhā*. This is the seal and mantra.
It enables the holder to realize the great gate of liberation, the Dharma of the Deathless (*amṛta*).
Next is the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Staff (*khakkhara*):
first, with the thumb of the right hand.
Stretching it across, place it in the palm.
With the index, ring, and little fingers, firmly clench them into a fist;
bend the elbow so that the palm is held level in front of the body and extended straight.
With his left hand, he grasps the corner of the *kāṣāya* robe,
with four inches of it protruding;
he likewise bends his elbow and extends it forward level with his chest.
The mantra is as follows: Homage as before.
Oṃ dūnā-codaraṇa hūṃ. This dhāraṇī-mantra accomplishes roots of goodness and fulfills compassionate vows.
If one encounters any malevolent sentient beings,
one should then form this mudrā to protect the body.
Next is the mantra and mudrā of the Great Dharma Conch (Mahādharmaśaṅkha).
With concentration and wisdom, join the palms with an empty mind; bend the *vāyu* (ring) and *ākāśa* (little finger) fingers so they cross at their tips.
The mantra is as before: "I take refuge.
Whisper it near the mouth and blow upon it.
Rotate to the left and right in the manner of blowing a conch shell; next is the fundamental emanation mudrā of Vairocana.
Join the thumb and ring finger of the samādhi hand, and do the same with the wisdom hand.
The two hands are joined with the palms facing upward;
the remaining three fingers—earth, fire, and wind—are spread apart and held upright.
The mantra of Śākyamuni Buddha is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ bhasma-kṣepa-naiḥsvabhāva-sarvadharmā-vastu-pratibhāsa-gaganasama svāhā.* With this mantra, recite with focused concentration and praise the Saṃbhogakāya as follows:

Vāme gajirasaṭa piṇāni sutana svāhaṃ pāśaka hasata bṛkucchi mukhake kara kṣaṃ jaḥ siddhiye dīve kīrṇa varipratī saṃstu ta svāhaṃ āliṅgana manīya ajara cchinnan mi dhyāna. [The ritual for making offerings, requesting [the deity to remain], and sending [the deity away].]
All should be practiced according to the Tathāgata family,
as explained in the Susiddhi and other texts,
taking Buddhalocanā as the family mother (kulamātṛ).

Having performed the protection ritual with the wrathful deity Durjaya as the vidyārāja—also known as Aparājita—one should thus exhort [the practitioner] to practice, and then depart from the maṇḍala.
Thereafter, while reciting the Mahāyāna heart-mantra, one should constantly maintain the mind upon the single reality (*ekasatya*).
Because there is no interruption, this Dharma is easily accomplished.
The teaching of the subtle Vajrayāna of Śākyamuni is hereby concluded.
*Śākyamunibuddha*, one fascicle.
